title: Mexico pauses at 7% as core inflation shifts the convergence date
summary: Banco de México unanimously interrupted its rate-cutting cycle on 5 February, keeping the overnight target at 7.00%. The decision turned on the persistence the Board now saw in core prices and the uncertainty surrounding fiscal changes at the start of 2026. A stronger peso and weak activity favoured disinflation, but neither had prevented an upward revision to inflation stretching into early 2027. The Board said it would consider further adjustments, with the rate consistent with a sustained return to 3%. It supplied no date, size or direction for a next move in that guidance. The voting record establishes agreement on a pause at this meeting (decision and guidance, p. 2).

The headline rate had edged down from 3.80% in November to 3.77% in the first half of January. The change chiefly reflected lower non-core inflation. Over the same endpoints, core inflation rose from 4.43% to 4.47%, after a December reading of 4.33%. Thus the small change for headline inflation conceals renewed underlying pressure. Expectations for headline inflation at the end of 2026 had risen, and longer-term expectations remained relatively stable above target. The announcement provides neither the size of those increases nor a decomposition of expectations into pricing and risk premia. Its most direct evidence that the change was material for policy is the Board’s own forecast revision (p. 1).

The table on p. 2 distinguishes quarterly averages of annual inflation from the annualised quarter-on-quarter changes shown in its memorandum rows. In the February forecast, the annual headline rates for 2026 Q1–Q4 were 4.0%, 3.8%, 3.6% and 3.5%. The December forecast had been 3.7%, 3.3%, 3.0% and 3.0%. The largest revision, 0.6 percentage points, was in the third quarter. For core inflation, the new quarterly sequence was 4.4%, 4.0%, 3.6% and 3.4%, against 4.0%, 3.4%, 3.0% and 3.0% previously. Both headline and core were now projected to reach 3.0% in the second quarter of 2027. These are changes between two forecast vintages. The 4.4% figure for core in the first quarter is a projected quarterly average of annual rates, distinct from the observed 4.47% in the first fortnight of January. The table notes that February’s projection begins in January and identifies INEGI as the source of observed annual inflation.

The memorandum rows give a further reason to avoid treating a falling annual rate as evidence of a uniformly benign month-to-month process. Annualised, seasonally adjusted headline inflation was projected at 4.1% in the first quarter and 4.0% in the second, even though the corresponding annual rates were projected to decline. The quarterly core measure was projected to ease from 4.2% to 3.3% over those two quarters. Part of the annual profile depends on the comparison period dropping out of the calculation. The Board expected services disinflation to proceed more gradually than previously assumed, and its projection already allowed for anticipated effects of the fiscal adjustments. It explicitly required further information to evaluate those effects comprehensively (pp. 1–2).

Financial and activity indicators pointed in the other direction. Mexican government yields had fallen across maturities since the previous policy decision and the peso had appreciated. Neither observation measures the immediate market reaction to this particular announcement. Domestic activity expanded in the fourth quarter after contracting in the third, but uncertainty and trade tensions still created downside risks. Abroad, global expansion appeared to be moderating, core inflation showed some persistence in major advanced economies, US government yields had moved within a limited range and the dollar had weakened. The Board treated changes in US economic policy as potentially inflationary or disinflationary for Mexico depending on their transmission. Its balance of risks had become more even, while retaining an upside bias: persistent core inflation, costs, depreciation, supply disruption and weather could delay convergence; weaker activity, lower cost pass-through or a stronger peso could accelerate it. For the future rate path, the evidence that would resolve the pause is how these opposing forces affect underlying prices after the initial fiscal adjustments, rather than a single favourable headline release.

questions.question: Are the fiscal adjustments changing the price level once or affecting subsequent price-setting?
questions.detail: The projection incorporates the expected effects but the Board says it cannot yet evaluate them fully. That distinction matters for the period over which policy must stay restrictive. Use detailed fortnightly CPI releases to compare directly affected items with subsequent price changes in related goods and services. Look to forthcoming Banco de México forecast analysis for its own separation of mechanical effects, second-round transmission and uncertainty.

questions.question: What would validate the slower projected decline in services inflation?
questions.detail: The Board identifies this persistence as one reason for an upward revision, but does not quantify the contribution of each service category. A broad, repeated acceleration would carry more information for the short-rate outlook than a seasonal reset in a few categories. Compare annual rates with successive seasonally adjusted quarterly measures, and inspect disaggregated INEGI services indices and the central bank’s own treatment of base effects.

questions.question: How much could a stronger peso or weaker domestic demand offset the new core trajectory?
questions.detail: Both appear on the downside of the Board’s risk assessment. The document provides no pass-through estimate, output-gap estimate or threshold at which either would outweigh cost pressures. Compare import-sensitive goods and domestically priced services alongside official activity indicators, then consult the central bank’s forecast sensitivities. This would help distinguish an exchange-rate improvement confined to tradables from a broader change in the balance of inflation risks.
